title: Variables and scope
notional_machine: A declaration creates a binding: a name attached to a value in one scope. let and const belong to the nearest enclosing block { } and cannot be read before their line runs; var belongs to the whole enclosing function (or module) and starts out as undefined. A name is looked up in the nearest scope first, then outward, and const stops the name being reassigned without freezing the value it holds.
steps: let x = 'outer' creates a binding named x in the module scope.
The if block opens a new scope. let x = 'inner' creates a second, separate x that shadows the outer one only inside the block.
var y ignores the block: it is created in the enclosing function (here the module), so it outlives the block.
After the block, looking up x finds the outer binding again and y is still visible, so it logs outer function-wide.

title: Functions and closures
notional_machine: Calling a function creates a fresh environment holding its parameters and local variables. A function created inside that call keeps a live link to that environment, not a copy of the values, so it reads and updates the variables as they are when it runs. Each call makes a new environment, and a function whose body is in { } returns undefined unless it reaches a return.
steps: makeCounter() runs and creates an environment holding count = 0. The arrow function it returns, a, keeps a link to that environment.
The second call creates a separate environment with its own count = 0, linked to b.
a() runs twice, raising a's count to 1 and then 2, so the second call returns 2.
b() raises only b's count, from 0 to 1, so the line logs 2 1.

title: Arrays and iteration
notional_machine: map, filter, and forEach call your function once for each element, in index order. map and filter build and return a new array and leave the original alone; forEach returns undefined and is only for side effects. push, splice, reverse, and sort change the array in place, and sort with no compare function compares elements as strings.
steps: map calls the arrow function with 10, 20, and 30 in turn and puts each result into a new array: [ 20, 40, 60 ].
filter calls its function with each element and keeps the ones where it returns true: [ 20, 30 ].
Neither method touches prices, so it still holds [ 10, 20, 30 ].

title: Loop bounds
notional_machine: An array of length n has indexes 0 to n - 1, so the last element is at n - 1 and nothing is at n. A loop for (let i = a; i < b; i++) runs b - a times, with i going from a up to b - 1, and changing < to <= adds one more run. slice(start, end) follows the same rule: it includes start and stops before end.
steps: xs.length is 3, so the valid indexes are 0, 1, and 2.
The loop runs while i < 3, so i takes the values 0, 1, and 2: three runs, which is 3 - 0.
When i becomes 3 the condition is false, so the loop stops before reading xs[3], which does not exist.

title: Objects and references
notional_machine: An object or array lives in one place in memory, and a variable holds a reference to it, like an arrow pointing at it. Assigning or passing the variable copies the arrow, so both names reach the same object, and === on objects compares arrows, not contents. Spread ({ ...obj } or [...arr]) makes a new outer object but copies the references inside it, so nested objects are still shared.
steps: { n: 1 } is created once in memory, and a holds a reference to it.
const b = a copies the reference, so b.n = 2 changes the one object both names point to.
{ ...a } creates a second object and copies the property n = 2 into it; c points at the new object.
c.n = 3 changes only the copy, so the line logs 2 2 3.

title: Truthiness and equality
notional_machine: === compares type and value and never converts. == first converts both sides to a common type, usually numbers, and then compares, so '1' == 1 is true. In an if, a ternary, or with || and &&, a value is converted to a boolean: only false, 0, '', null, undefined, and NaN are falsy, and everything else, including '0', [], and {}, is truthy.
steps: '1' == 1 converts the string '1' to the number 1 before comparing, so it is true.
'1' === 1 compares a string with a number without converting, so it is false.
'' is one of the few falsy values, so Boolean('') is false.
'0' is a non-empty string and [] is an object, so both are truthy.

title: Async basics
notional_machine: JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time. The current synchronous code always runs to the end first; then queued promise callbacks run (then callbacks and the code after an await), and only after those do timer callbacks run, even setTimeout(fn, 0). await pauses only the async function it is in and hands control back to its caller until the promise settles.
steps: console.log('A') runs immediately.
setTimeout queues its callback as a timer task; nothing runs yet.
then queues its callback as a promise job; nothing runs yet.
console.log('D') runs, and the synchronous code is finished.
Promise jobs run before timer tasks, so C logs, then B.
